newsitem.title: UK: Young British criminals set to be tagged.
newsitem.headline: Young British criminals set to be tagged.

text.p: British courts could order electronic tagging of juvenile offenders as young as 10 years of age under a bill going through parliament, a government minister said on Thursday.
"Juveniles can already be subject to a curfew as part of a supervision order, but only in the evening and at night," said Home Office minister David Maclean.
"Electronic monitoring will detect immediately whether the offender is breaking the curfew."
Pilot schemes for the electronic monitoring of curfew orders for offenders aged 16 and above have been running in Britain since July 1995.

Tackling juvenile crime and raising moral standards amongst Britain's youth is a hot political issue for both the ruling Conservative party and opposition Labour ahead of the general election which must take place by May next year.
The new bill before parliament would give courts in selected areas the power to impose a curfew and electronic tagging on offenders aged from 10 to 15.

The tagging proposal comes on the heels of a public spending watchdog report out on Thursday which said the justice system for juveniles was in disarray and failing to cut crime despite costing one billion pounds ($1.68 billion) a year.
An 18-month study by the government-funded Audit Commission said only three percent of the estimated seven million crimes committed by 10 to 17 year olds each year lead to an arrest.
A penal reform pressure group on Thursday condemned the plans to extend tagging to children under the age of 16.
"This is one of the worst ideas yet to tackle juvenile crime," said Paul Cavadino, chairman of the Penal Affairs Consortium.
Cavadino said the government was using the scheme to score political points.
"It suggests that the government is more concerned to appear tough than to examine hard evidence about which measures work best in preventing reoffending." ($1=.5940 Pound)
